meta.title: Chronicle
meta.dek: chronicle turns a brief and the facts behind it into an illustrated, interactive web page made for its subject. Claude writes the story and draws the pictures; code computes every number, checks the page and paints the drawings in watercolor. It went from first commit to version {{release.version|plain}} in {{release.days}}, with {{tests.passed}} passing.
byline: Prepared for developers and IT leadership
Built with chronicle from its own repository
meta.description: An executive overview of the chronicle plugin: the problem it solves, where teams use it, how it works and what it runs on, built with chronicle itself.
meta.colophon:
This page was built by chronicle {{release.version|plain}} from its own repository. The facts file holds every figure, read from the code, the git history, the RFCs and a test run on {{release.as_of|date}}; hover or tap a figure to see its source. The two paintings were drawn as SVG for this page and painted by the plugin's OpenCV painter. The architecture animation is one SVG with no script, built by `chronicle animate`.

Token figures are estimates from {{rfc.story_rfc}}. Build timings come from one run on a cloud container and will differ on other machines.

chapters.title: Status pages are assembled by hand, and their numbers lose their sources

blocks.text:
Every review cycle, someone opens GitHub, Jira, Confluence and Datadog in separate tabs, copies the numbers into a slide template and adds them up by hand. The deck is out of date by the meeting. Nobody can say where a figure came from, and next quarter the work starts again from a blank template.

Asking a language model to write the page moves the problem without solving it. The model types numbers from memory, quality varies from page to page, and each page costs several times the tokens. {{rfc.story_rfc}} rejected that route for those three reasons.

blocks.caption: The hand-built status deck: four tools pinned to the board, a figure cut out and glued onto a slide, and the questions every reviewer asks.

spots.label: Four tools
spots.title: Four tools, four tabs
spots.text: The facts live in GitHub, Jira, Confluence and Datadog. A person copies each one into the deck by hand.

spots.label: No source
spots.title: No source, no date
spots.text: A pasted figure carries no source, no as-of date and no record of the arithmetic behind it.

spots.label: Every cycle
spots.title: Cut and paste, every cycle
spots.text: Nothing carries over. Next quarter the same person repeats the same copying.

blocks.text: Custom pages show the same cost in code. Before the third release, a golf-simulator handbook built on chronicle still needed {{evidence.hand_css}} of hand-written CSS and about {{evidence.hand_js}} of script to look like its subject. A podcast guide written by hand outside chronicle carried over {{evidence.podcast_figures}}. Each later release moved that kind of work into the theme and the blocks.

chapters.title: One engine serves the steering committee, the new hire and the slide deck

blocks.text: chronicle reads its facts from connected tools ({{features.connectors}}: GitHub, Jira, Confluence, Datadog and PagerDuty) or from pasted notes, files and transcripts. The same builder then shapes the page for its forum, and the skill carries a chapter outline for each one. {{features.examples}} with invented data ship with the plugin to show the range.

chapters.kicker: What a Claude Code plugin is
chapters.title: chronicle is one Claude Code plugin with two skills and a subagent

blocks.text: A Claude Code plugin is a directory of skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers or other components that Claude Code installs and loads as one unit. A manifest at `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` gives the plugin its name, and can add a version, a description and other metadata. Each component adds one kind of thing to a session, and chronicle uses three of them.

blocks.title: What a plugin can hold, and what chronicle uses
columns: What it adds to a session
rows: The plugin's name, version and description
Instructions Claude loads when a request fits; people can also run each one as a command
A subagent Claude can delegate work to, in its own context
Commands Claude Code runs at lifecycle events, such as after every edit
Tool servers that give Claude new tools while the plugin is enabled
None; the gatherer uses the servers the session already has

blocks.title: One directory, and what each file becomes in a session
blocks.subtitle: Drawn after the plugin diagram in the Claude Code docs. Step through the components, or hover a box.
blocks.alt: Diagram in two columns joined by five arrows. Left, the plugins/chronicle directory: .claude-plugin/plugin.json, skills/story/SKILL.md, skills/animation/SKILL.md, agents/chronicle-gatherer.md, and scripts/chronicle with src/chronicle. Right, what each becomes in a session: the plugin name chronicle with its version, the skills /chronicle:story and /chronicle:animation, a subagent that gathers facts read-only, and a builder the skills run through Bash. The plugin has no hooks and no .mcp.json.

steps.title: Manifest
steps.text: `plugin.json` gives the plugin its name, version and description. The marketplace entry points Claude Code at this folder.

steps.title: Skills
steps.text: Each `SKILL.md` runs as a command, and Claude also loads it when a request matches its description.

steps.title: Subagent
steps.text: The gatherer runs in its own context with the session's MCP servers and hands back only a facts file.

steps.title: Builder
steps.text: The Python builder is plain files inside the plugin. The skills call it at the plugin root, so it installs and updates with them.

blocks.text:
Plugins travel through marketplaces. A marketplace is a repository with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` that lists plugins and where to fetch each one; it is a catalog, and nothing is hosted. This repository is the 10x-agent-marketplace, and it lists {{marketplace.plugins}}. A teammate adds it once with `/plugin marketplace add jacquelineadean/10x-agent-marketplace`, then runs `/plugin install chronicle@10x-agent-marketplace`.

Skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers all work on their own. A plugin packages several of them as one unit, with one install command, versioned releases and updates from the marketplace. chronicle needs that packaging: its two skills, the gatherer and {{code.py_now|compact}} of Python builder code must move together, or a skill would call a builder that does not match it. The [Claude Code plugins overview](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/overview) covers the format in full.

blocks.title: What an enabled plugin adds to every session

MCP servers run alongside each session, and hooks fire at their events
None: chronicle defines no hooks and no MCP servers

User, project or local install; cloud sessions load their own plugins

chapters.title: The model writes and draws; code computes, checks and paints

blocks.text: A run lives in one local folder and moves through seven steps. Claude settles the brief with the author, hands fact gathering to a subagent, designs the page's identity, draws each illustration as SVG and writes the story. Code does everything that has a right answer: the arithmetic, the checks, the painting and the HTML. The author confirms before anything leaves the machine.

blocks.title: Who does each step, by hand and with chronicle
blocks.subtitle: Switch between the two ways of making the page, or select a step for what happens in it.

nodes.label: Gather
nodes.text: The `chronicle-gatherer` subagent queries connected tools read-only, asks for counts and aggregates, and writes facts.json. Its raw tool output stays inside the subagent.

nodes.label: Compute
nodes.text: Averages, ratios, percent changes and burnup forecasts are entries in the derive table. Code computes them before the page is checked, so the prose and the charts agree.

nodes.label: Design
nodes.text: Claude writes a one-sentence concept, then the palette, fonts from a list of {{features.fonts}}, a progress bar, chapter marks and the words on every control.

nodes.label: Draw
nodes.text: Claude draws each picture as plain SVG: shapes back to front, ink outlines and live text labels that can hold facts.

nodes.label: Paint
nodes.text: The painter turns each drawing into ink and watercolor: washes with wet edges, granulation and pen lines that overshoot. A full Keystone build painted {{bench.keystone_plates}} in {{bench.keystone_seconds}}.

nodes.label: Check
nodes.text: Unknown tokens stop the build. Numbers typed into prose, drawings outside the SVG allowlist and widget scripts that reach for the network are flagged first.

nodes.label: Publish
nodes.text: The skill asks once before publishing data from company systems. The page goes to claude.ai as a private Artifact, and republishing keeps the same link.

blocks.title: Inside chronicle build
blocks.subtitle: Hover or tap a box for detail, or step through the build.
blocks.alt: Diagram: facts.json, story.json and the SVG drawings feed four stages in order: derive, check, paint and render. The build folder holds artifact.html and the paintings as WebP. An error at the check stops the build; unchanged drawings are not repainted.

steps.title: Derive
steps.text: Code runs the derive table: {{features.derive_fns}} compute every total, share, ratio and forecast from the gathered series.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: The check stops on unknown tokens, warns on numbers typed into prose, sanitizes every drawing and lints every widget script.

steps.title: Paint
steps.text: NumPy and OpenCV paint each drawing in ink and watercolor; a drawing that has not changed is not repainted.

steps.title: Render
steps.text: The standard-library renderer writes static HTML for every word plus one JSON blob; a vanilla script draws the charts.

blocks.title: The rule
blocks.text: Give the model the data and let code do the arithmetic. A figure enters the page only as a token, so every number on it traces back to a source.

chapters.title: Everything runs on the author's machine until the author publishes

blocks.text: chronicle follows the repository's command-line layout. Pure rules with no I/O sit in `core/`. Every file read, browser call and video encode sits in `connectors/`, and the command line in `entrypoints/` wires them together. Rendering uses the Python standard library only. NumPy and OpenCV are the {{controls.runtime_deps}} the painter needs, and uv fetches them into its own cache without touching the user's Python.

blocks.title: The architecture, step by step
blocks.subtitle: The plugin's own design as an animated technical architecture diagram (TAD), built by chronicle animate. Pause shows the still.

data.alt: The story skill delegates to a read-only gatherer that turns connected tools into a facts file; Claude writes the story and drawings; chronicle build derives, checks, paints and renders on the author's machine; the page publishes as a private Artifact only after the author confirms.
data.note: One SVG with no script. The same build exports a GIF and an MP4 for slides.
steps: The author's brief starts the story skill: the audience, the point, the window and the sources.
A gatherer subagent queries connected tools read-only and writes only the facts file; raw tool output never reaches the main conversation.
Claude writes the story and draws each picture as SVG; numbers enter only as tokens that point into the facts file.
chronicle build derives every computed number, checks the story, paints each drawing and renders one page.
After a screenshot review and the author's go-ahead, the page publishes as a private Artifact.
Until that publish, every fact and file stays in a git-ignored folder on the author's machine.

chapters.title: Company data stays local and read-only until a person publishes it

blocks.text: The design assumes a page will hold company data and that text from source tools cannot be trusted. Each risk below has a control, and the strongest controls run inside the build, so a page that breaks them does not build.

blocks.text:
**The ask.** Approve or amend {{rfc.story_rfc}} to {{rfc.last_rfc}}, starting with the runtime packages and the two Constitution amendments, which every later release builds on. The four RFCs list {{rfc.open_questions}} in all; the table holds the ones that change what ships.

Next, from the RFCs' own lists: a browser test suite for the page script, which Python tests of the HTML and data cover today only indirectly; PDF or slide export; and turning photographs into watercolors for team pages.
